title: Market division when output needs sunk capacity
question: Does the tacit market division seen in a bare two-good Cournot game survive, strengthen or vanish when each firm must build and pay for production capacity before it can sell?
hypothesis: Sunk capacity makes division more stable: firms specialise as often as in the bare game, specialise earlier in build choices than in quantities, and re-enter a market even less often because re-entry costs machines.
test: Run the same two-firm, two-good market twice: as Lin et al.'s bare quantity game, and inside the factory world with identical demand curves and variable costs, where quantities are capped by machines the firm has built. Match model, temperature, horizon (unknown to agents), memory format and seeds. Score each run once on final-quarter HHI per good and the round at which each firm's build mix becomes specialised.
baseline: Bare Cournot game with the same demand and costs; scripted Cournot-Nash firms in the factory world.
metrics: Round of build specialisation vs round of quantity specialisation
falsifier: Division rates in the factory world are no higher than in the bare game and specialisation does not appear in builds before quantities.
confounds: The factory prompt is longer and the action space larger, which can lower competence rather than change incentives. Capacity limits can force specialisation mechanically if starting cash cannot fund both lines; set starting cash so both lines are affordable.

prior.relation: Source result: division in a bare two-good Cournot game without communication.
Replication with capacity constraints but no build decisions or production chain.
Adds cost-reducing investment to Cournot; prices up to 200% of Nash in LLM-LLM markets. Not market division across goods.

needs: Pick the simulator (own Python world or FLE layer) and fix demand, cost and starting-cash values from a scripted-agent pilot.

title: Firms per good and the collapse of division
question: How does tacit division change as the number of firms rises relative to the number of goods?
hypothesis: Division holds while firms do not outnumber goods and breaks toward Cournot-Nash quantities once they do, because a clean one-firm-per-good split no longer exists.
test: Factorial over firms N in {2,3,4,6} and goods M in {2,3}, same per-good demand scaled so the monopoly quantity per good is constant. Same model across firms. Score run-level mean HHI and profit gap fraction.
baseline: Scripted Cournot-Nash firms at each N and M; the N=2, M=2 cell as the Lin et al. reference.
metrics: Profit as fraction of Nash-to-monopoly gap
Share of runs with a stable one-firm-per-good split
falsifier: Division or supra-competitive profit persists at N > M at rates similar to N <= M.
confounds: More firms means longer prompts and more history per round; hold history length fixed in tokens. Run cost grows with N; budget seeds per cell from a pilot.

prior.relation: Pricing game: three sellers can collude, four unstable, five never reach sustained collusion.
Dutch-auction bidders collude only when few.
Only N = M = 2 tested.

needs: A pilot to size seeds per cell; decide whether M > 3 is worth the extra recipes.

title: One principal, several firms
question: Does a principal that runs k of N firms earn more than the same principal running one firm with k times the starting capital, and how do the independent firms respond?
hypothesis: Splitting pays: the Sybil cluster takes a larger combined output share and profit than the merged firm, and divides goods internally with no visible coordination, while independent firms end up with less than in a market of N independents.
test: N = 4 firms. Arms: four independents; one principal with two firms plus two independents (with and without a private back-channel between the principal's firms, and with a shared or separate objective); the principal as one firm with double capital plus two independents. Same model throughout. Score principal profit, independents' profit and HHI per run.
baseline: Four independent firms; the merged double-capital firm.
metrics: Principal's combined profit and output share
falsifier: The principal's split firms earn no more than the merged firm, or behave no differently from two independent firms.
confounds: Two firms get two prompts and twice the inference per round; match total tokens or report both. Shared objective and back-channel are separate effects; cross them. Classic Cournot theory already predicts gains from splitting under linear demand, so the result to look for is whether LLM firms exploit it and how the others react.

prior.relation: Vending-Bench Arena ran team rounds, the closest prior, but left them out of the analysis; environment not public.
Theory of the cost of Sybils and false-name-proof mechanisms; no LLM market test.
Citation follow-up found no work with one principal controlling several firms in this game.

needs: A sybil-resistance or agent-markets survey to the gate; a principled token-matching rule across arms.

title: Telling Sybil firms from tacit colluders
question: Can an auditor that sees only market data and build logs identify which firms share an owner, and does it confuse Sybil clusters with independent firms that colluded tacitly?
hypothesis: Concentration-based detectors flag both, so they confuse Sybils with tacit colluders; build-graph features (timing of builds, complementary patch claims) separate them better than quantities alone.
test: Pool runs from MKT-01 to MKT-03 with ground-truth owner labels. Train or tune detectors on some operators and seeds, test on held-out ones: (a) quantity and HHI features in the style of Bracale-Syrnikov's oracle, (b) strategy-graph features, (c) build-log features. Score pairwise same-owner AUC and the false-positive rate on tacitly colluding independent pairs.
falsifier: Build-log features add no AUC over quantity features, or detectors already separate Sybils from tacit colluders without them.
confounds: If Sybil firms share a prompt they may share style; vary prompts within a principal. Labels must never reach the detector through file names or ordering.

prior.relation: Oracle detects coordination from quantities; does not distinguish ownership from tacit collusion.
Auditing collusion from queried strategy graphs; no Sybil labels.
Collusion detection with unknown colluding subgroups, from activations rather than market data.

needs: Enough labelled runs from MKT-03; a held-out split by principal, not by round.

title: Reading the messages versus reading the market
question: When firms can talk, does reading their messages and stated plans detect collusion better than action-based signals?
hypothesis: Text detectors catch explicit proposals but miss tacit division and flag talk that never becomes action; action-based detectors beat them on run-level collusion.
test: Runs with public and private chat. A text classifier (LLM judge blind to outcomes) and an action detector (profit gap, HHI, build specialisation) each label every run; score both against an outcome-defined collusion label set before analysis.
baseline: Action detector alone; text detector alone.
metrics: Run-level precision and recall per detector
Share of runs with collusive talk but competitive actions
Share with collusive actions but no collusive talk
falsifier: The text detector matches or beats the action detector on runs without explicit proposals.
confounds: The judge model may share biases with firm models; use a different family. Defining collusion from outcomes makes the action detector partly circular; also report against a profitable-deviation check.

prior.relation: Finds 'collusion on paper': agents plan collusion in text but act otherwise.
Reasoning faithfulness does not predict collusion.
Argues steered collusion cannot be spotted from reasoning text.

needs: Fix the outcome definition of collusion before any labelled run.

title: No channel, public channel, private channel
question: How does the communication channel (none, one public board, private pairwise messages) change division, price level and explicit price-fixing in a production market?
hypothesis: Any channel raises supra-competitive profit; private messages raise explicit carve-up proposals most, while a public board yields similar division with fewer explicit proposals.
test: Three-arm comparison at N = 3, M = 3, same model, matched message budget per round. Score run-level profit gap, HHI and the rate of explicit coordination proposals coded by a blind judge.
falsifier: Profit gap and HHI do not differ between arms.
confounds: Messages consume context; pad the no-channel arm with neutral text of matched length.

prior.relation: Double auctions: seller communication raises collusion.
Private emails among firms; 12.6% misaligned including price-fixing.
Price collusion in Bertrand without a channel.

needs: Message budget and judge rubric fixed before runs.

title: Forked firms and inherited conventions
question: Do two firms forked from one agent mid-game, sharing its memory, divide markets faster than two independent firms of the same model, and does a merger of rivals carry a collusive convention into a new market?
hypothesis: Forks inherit a plan and divide almost at once; after a merger, the surviving memory imposes its earlier convention on new rivals.
test: Arms: fork a firm at round r into two (copied notes, split assets) vs spawn a fresh firm with the same assets; separately, merge two firms that had divided one market and place the merged firm in a new market with fresh rivals. Score rounds to stable division and HHI after the event.
baseline: Fresh-firm entry with the same assets; a merged firm whose memory is wiped.
metrics: Rounds to stable division after fork
HHI after fork and after merger
Share of post-merger runs reproducing the earlier split
falsifier: Forks divide no faster than fresh firms and merged memory does not change the new market's outcome.
confounds: Copied memory also copies competence; compare with a fork that copies only general notes, not plans.

prior.relation: Keeping the same partner raises prices even without punishment; persistence, not forking.
A shared optimised prompt for both firms produces stable collusion.
Uses a plans-and-insights memory like the one a fork would copy.

needs: A precise fork and merge primitive (what is copied, how assets split) written before runs.

title: Mixed models as a natural brake
question: Do markets with firms from different model families divide less than same-model markets?
hypothesis: Mixed-family markets divide less and sit closer to Cournot-Nash, but the effect is smaller than the effect of adding a firm.
test: N = 3 firms; arms: all one family, two plus one, three families. Rotate families across positions. Score run-level HHI and profit gap.
baseline: Same-family markets for each family used.
falsifier: Mixed markets divide as often as same-family ones.
confounds: Families differ in competence; a weak firm can look competitive simply by mistake. Report each firm's best-response error against scripted rivals.

prior.relation: Heterogeneity in patience or data cuts the collusive price lift from 22% to 7-10%.
Mixing models in auctions does not reliably reduce collusion.
Includes cross-provider duopolies.

needs: Decide which families are affordable at the needed run count.

title: Public production ledger
question: Does publishing each firm's output and capacity every round raise tacit division compared with showing only market totals?
hypothesis: A public per-firm ledger raises division and profit gap, because firms can see and respect each other's territory.
test: Two arms at N = 3: firms see only own data and market totals (Lin et al.'s information set) vs a public ledger of every firm's quantities and machines. Same model and seeds.
falsifier: The ledger arm shows no more division than the own-data arm.
confounds: The ledger lengthens the prompt; pad the other arm.

prior.relation: Agents see only own quantity, price, share and profit.
Prices rise even when rival prices are hidden.
Firms see competitors' prices and stock.

needs: Maps to budget hunch B4 (tacit cartels via a public ledger); align with BUD candidates before promotion.

title: One competitive entrant
question: Does a single scripted competitive firm entering mid-game break an established division?
hypothesis: A best-response entrant breaks division in the good it enters and pushes incumbents toward Cournot quantities there, but incumbents keep their split in other goods.
test: After division forms, add a scripted Cournot best-response firm (or a provably non-colluding learner) in one good. Compare with adding an LLM firm of the same model.
metrics: HHI in entered vs other goods
Rounds until a new division forms
falsifier: Division in the entered good survives the scripted entrant.
confounds: Entry adds capacity and lowers prices mechanically; compare against the Cournot prediction with N+1 firms.

prior.relation: Theory: one defector can break collusion.
Adding an entrant works better than a prompt warning in an LLM pricing replication.
A class of learners that provably cannot collude; a clean control firm.

needs: Decide entry timing rule (fixed round vs after division is detected).

title: Sybils against an antitrust regulator
question: Under a regulator that fines detected collusion from market concentration, does a principal running several firms keep its gains by spreading output across identities?
hypothesis: A concentration-based regulator lowers tacit collusion among independents but not the Sybil principal's gains, because spreading output keeps each firm's share below the trigger.
test: Cross the MKT-03 arms with a Bracale-Syrnikov-style oracle-plus-fines regime. Score principal and independent profit with and without the regulator.
metrics: Principal profit with vs without regulator
falsifier: The regulator cuts the principal's gains as much as it cuts independents' collusion.
confounds: Fine size and trigger set the result; sweep at least two trigger levels.

prior.relation: Oracle plus fines cuts severe collusion from 50% to 5.6%; no Sybils.
False-name-proof mechanism theory.
Team rounds unanalysed.

needs: MKT-03 first; regulator parameters copied from Bracale-Syrnikov where possible.

title: Does the small simulator predict the real game
question: Do division and Sybil effects found in a small Python factory simulation reappear when the same markets sit on top of the Factorio Learning Environment?
hypothesis: The direction of effects carries over but their size shrinks, because agents in the full game spend most effort on building rather than strategy.
test: Pick the two strongest effects from the small simulator. Add a market layer (demand curves, per-firm sales and profit) to FLE's multi-agent mode and rerun those comparisons at small N with matched demand.
metrics: Share of rounds with failed builds
falsifier: Effects reverse or vanish in FLE while the agents still build working factories.
confounds: FLE agents take turns rather than act at once; simulate simultaneous selling by revealing sales only after all firms submit.

prior.relation: FLE paper; single-agent experiments only.
Multi-agent mode since v0.2 with messaging and impostor tasks; no markets.
Gather-trade-build economy where agents specialise; RL agents, not LLMs.

needs: Confirm a headless Factorio server can run on team hardware and what FLE's market layer would take.

title: Market limits with uncertain ownership and concurrent settlement
question: Which aggregate spending and concentration protections survive inaccurate ownership records and concurrent actions that are individually permitted?
hypothesis: Unreviewed hunch: Atomic checks over a common resource ledger preserve declared aggregate spending limits under complete mediation, but owner-specific concentration limits fail under missed owner links; conservative grouping trades those failures for false restrictions on independent firms.
test: Extend Patchwork market conformance with paired prohibited and benign action sets. Randomize independent market episodes across local checks, per-agent checks, causal provenance and atomic aggregate-state checks. Independently vary proposal concurrency and observed ownership errors: missed same-owner links, false merges of independent firms and unresolved owners. Keep true ownership in the evaluator and identical observed records across comparable policies; oracle ownership is a separate ceiling. First replay fixed scripted proposals to isolate enforcement, then run a separately qualified model pilot with matched total compute per principal and neutral profit objectives. Measure attempted versus committed violations separately; do not infer agent discovery from scripted strategies.
baseline: Perfect-owner atomic enforcement, merged firm with the same capital, genuinely independent firms with matched actions, and non-atomic aggregate checks exposed to the same interleavings.
falsifier: Practical observed-owner policies match the oracle across prespecified missing-link and false-merge conditions with no meaningful utility loss, or causal-only review enforces the chosen aggregate limits without equivalent shared-state accounting.
confounds: Knowing beneficial owners solves an identity problem by assumption. Complete mediation and atomic settlement are prerequisites, not model behavior. Conservation alone is not fair allocation; equal per-firm inference can advantage owners with more identities.

prior.relation: Local scripted suite left 200/500 prohibited cases under causal provenance and zero under aggregate invariants; owner labels and settlement were trusted.
Catalogue records budget conservation under mediation, authentication and crash-fault assumptions; it does not establish resistance to false beneficial-owner labels.
False-name mechanism theory motivates matching principal resources; it supplies no general ownership-inference solution.

needs: Enumerate the exact invariants and legal observations, freeze ownership-error generation and qualify race controls. Connect to MKT-03/MKT-11 and BUD-08/BUD-09 while keeping enforcement correctness separate from incentives and discovery.

title: Evidence royalties versus identity farming
question: Can paying for evidence used in a joint opportunity increase useful discovery without making duplicate identities or redundant evidence more profitable?
hypothesis: Unreviewed hunch: In repeated private-profit worlds with costly discovery, payments tied to unique evidence actually used increase useful evidence production and producer returns relative to free reuse; payments per publisher instead reward duplicated identities and redundant claims.
test: Modify the Patchwork economy to make discovery costly and allow agents to choose whether to search and publish across repeated opportunities. Randomize whole market episodes to free public reuse, a fixed revenue share divided among all publishers, or the same share divided among unique evidence receipts used at settlement. Cross a single owner versus permitted identity splitting at matched capital, total model budget and discovery opportunities; keep evidence visibility and communication channels identical in the main comparison. Preregister how substitutes and complementary evidence share payment and how duplicate receipts are rejected. Observe endogenous discovery as well as completion, owner-level payoffs and unused contributions. A separate matched visibility control should test whether public evidence, rather than chat, carries coordination.
baseline: Original free-reuse economy, publisher-count royalties, no-splitting arms and scripted policies showing each payment rule is executable; all transfers come from the same realized revenue, not added subsidy.
metrics: Unique useful evidence produced per opportunity
Opportunity completion and net external surplus
Redundant claims, contracts and payment concentration
falsifier: At prespecified precision, receipt-based payments do not improve discovery or producer returns, lose comparable net surplus through friction, or permit profitable identity splitting without new useful evidence.
confounds: The old nine-case pilot never tested royalties. Recorded use is not causal marginal contribution or moral entitlement; substitute and complementary evidence complicate attribution. An oracle deduplicator hides manipulation, and changing evidence visibility together with payments confounds incentives.

prior.relation: Nine economy cases used no service contracts; four of six sales were solo with freely reusable public evidence. This motivates but does not establish a property-rights mechanism.
Catalogue documents model-dependent free-riding in public-goods games, a different institution from evidence production; it does not predict this treatment effect.
Shows why counting identities in rewards can introduce false-name incentives; no blanket guarantee transfers to evidence royalties.

needs: Specify discovery costs, payment conservation, observable evidence receipts and a non-oracle deduplication comparator; resolve Patchwork access and complete the relevant survey/review gates. Related to BUD-14, MKT-09 and SEC-14, but tests compensation for information production.
